Photograph in a series which records and documents the photographer's brother, carver Hideta Kitazawa, making a Japanese noh mask for the Pitt Rivers Museum [2015.28], commissioned as part of the VERVE Project to be exhibited in a new case display on the subject of 'Woodworking': 'The Wood (Hinoki)/ I use Hinoki wood (Japanese Cypress) for making noh masks. It is found only in one small mountainous, deep valley region in Japan, called Kiso, located near Nagoya. Kiso's harsh climate (with a lot of snow in winter) causes the Japanese Cypress tree to grow very slowly and produces beautiful annual rings. We usually use Hinoki wood that is approximately 200-300 years old and has been stored in suitably dry conditions. This means that the wood is both strong and lightweight./ The timber merchant that I use only supplies Hinoki wood. I have a very good relationship with this timber supplier - and they always supply me with the best quality wood' (caption provided by Hideta Kitazawa).

Photograph in a series which records and documents the photographer's brother, carver Hideta Kitazawa, making a Japanese noh mask for the Pitt Rivers Museum [2015.28], commissioned as part of the VERVE Project to be exhibited in a new case display on the subject of 'Woodworking': 'The first stage of Noh-mask making/ A basis pattern is copied onto a block of Hinoki wood (Japanese cypress). This picture shows the outline patterns, the block of Hinoki wood, and a range of my mask-making tools' (caption provided by Hideta Kitazawa).

Photograph in a series which records and documents the photographer's brother, carver Hideta Kitazawa, making a Japanese noh mask for the Pitt Rivers Museum [2015.28], commissioned as part of the VERVE Project to be exhibited in a new case display on the subject of 'Woodworking': 'The way I sharpen my chisels/ I use a whetstone, which is first soaked in water, to sharpen my chisels. There are different types of whetstone. I use a red stone (which is rough) initially, followed by a darker coloured stone, which is smoother, for finishing. These are natural stones found in Japan' (caption provided by Hideta Kitazawa).

Photograph in a series which records and documents the photographer's brother, carver Hideta Kitazawa, making a Japanese noh mask for the Pitt Rivers Museum [2015.28], commissioned as part of the VERVE Project to be exhibited in a new case display on the subject of 'Woodworking': 'The rough carving/ Two types of chisels are used in traditional Japanese style carving - the ends of the handles on my "rough carving chisels" have metal discs to protect them, as they are hit with a hammer./ For the rough carving stage I start carving from the nose, then move to eyes and the mouth - always bearing in mid the overall balance of the mask' (caption provided by Hideta Kitazawa).

Photograph in a series which records and documents the photographer's brother, carver Hideta Kitazawa, making a Japanese noh mask for the Pitt Rivers Museum [2015.28], commissioned as part of the VERVE Project to be exhibited in a new case display on the subject of 'Woodworking': 'Hideta Kitazawa/ Born: 4 February 1968/ Mask maker and Shinto Temple carver. Hideta chose to follow in his father's footsteps and become a second-generation woodcarving artist. In 1991, after graduating from the Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology with a major in Forestry Studies, he went on to begin intensive woodcarving studies with his father Ikkyou Kitazawa. Since then, he has been the recipient of a number of awards, including the "Outstanding Young Artisan Award" for Tokyo in 1997, and the Yokohama Noh Drama Theatre Director's Prize in 2003' (caption provided by Hideta Kitazawa).
